catalog_quote: [Magnusson [2008], sec. 6 TONE, p.17:] The tonology of the Bantu languages is generally a highly complex issue. According to Baucom (1972:53) differences in tone are often mentioned by Wambo speakers as the main differences between the dialects. In my view, the topic of tone would be best treated by a native speaker with linguistic training, a task that is still waiting for its man (or woman). [sec. 9:] It was mentioned to me once by a Kwambi man that there may be some tonal differences. In his case he was referring to differences between the people of Okatana in the east and Elim further west. new_statements.rule_in_words: Kwambi, like all Wambo (R.20) varieties, is reported (second-hand, via Halme citing Baucom) to have a two-tone (H/L) system; no source opened says anything about the position of word stress or accent in Kwambi. The only open primary description (Magnusson) treats segments and morphology and explicitly leaves tone undescribed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (Homburger 1949's generic 'In Bantu the dynamic accent is on the penultimate syllable in the southern..' is not tied to Kwambi and was seen only as a snippet.)
new_statements.domain_note: No word- vs phrase-level prominence statement exists in the opened material; the tone report is a family-level generalisation over all Wambo languages, not a Kwambi-specific analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: All material concerns Kwambi proper (Oshikwambi/Otshikwambi/'Ochikwambi', Uukwambi district, central Owambo; Glottolog kwam1251, ISO kwm, Guthrie R.23). Magnusson's corpus is mostly eastern and central Uukwambi (Okatana, Elim); he notes possible tonal differences east vs west and nasal-drop in the far-western Onaanda area. The tone statement found is a generalisation over all Wambo/R.20 varieties (Baucom via Halme), not Kwambi-specific.

new_statements.relation_note: Matches the existing statement exactly (it was built from the same archive.org snippet of this book): Kwambi is a Wambo language, all Wambo languages tonal per Baucom 1974 as reported by Halme; no word-stress placement anywhere. The extra Brincker fragment (penultimate 'accent') concerns Kwanyama, not Kwambi, so it does not change the Kwambi record. Full text not opened: the listed open_url is the publisher's sales page (PDF EUR 69.80; only the table of contents is free), the archive.org copy could not be reached by automated download (access-restricted), and HELDA has no record of the Helsinki dissertation version.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Kwambi the book gives no stress rule at all: Kwambi appears only in the list of twelve Wambo languages and in the vocabulary entry -kwambi/Ovakwambi 'Kwambi people'; the comparative chapter 7.1 treats Mbandja, Ndonga and Mbalanhu, not Kwambi. The only group-level statement covering Kwambi is second-hand (Baucom 1974): every Wambo language has two tone phonemes. The 'default place of the accent being the penultimate syllable' fragment is Halme's summary of Brincker's 1891 description of Kwanyama (R.21), where 'Accent/Ton' is Brincker's pre-tonal term; it is not a claim about Kwambi and not a modern stress statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned in any snippet or in the table of contents
new_statements.exceptions: For Kwanyama (Brincker, as summarised by Halme): 'variation in the placement of the accent of certain infinitives'. Nothing for Kwambi.
new_statements.identity_note: Halme 2004 describes Kwanyama (R.21, Angola/Namibia); Kwambi (R.23, Uukwambi, Namibia) is only named as one of the twelve Wambo languages and has no section of its own. The Brincker fragment is about Kwanyama specifically.

sources.note: Magnusson's Kwambi description is explicitly differential against Ndonga ('features which are not mentioned as being different are as described for the grammar.. of the closest literary dialect') and reports no prosodic difference; Fivaz's Ndonga grammar has a tone/length chapter and is the de facto statement of accent/penultimate behaviour that Kwambi would inherit by that method.
